current_episode.title: Women's Activewear: From Nursing to Founding a Colourful Running Brand with Nicky Chrascina #191

guest.bio_context: Nicky trained as a registered general nurse in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa, qualifying in 1984, then worked as a midwife before transitioning to pharmaceutical sales where she worked primarily in oncology hospital sales for approximately 25 years. She began running at age 23-24 after a bet with her father and has since completed over 156 ultras, marathons, and multi-day races. She founded Flancy Activewear nine years ago after becoming frustrated with the lack of colorful running apparel available in the market.

pending_qa.q: How did someone transition from being a non-runner to completing over 150 ultramarathons?
pending_qa.r: At age 23-24, Nicky made an offhand remark that she could run a marathon after watching her stepmother train for the Comrades Ultra Marathon in Swaziland, leading to a bet with her father for 100 rands. She entered the London Marathon in 1993, starting with minimal knowledge and a walk-one-lamppost, run-one-lamppost training approach, eventually completing her first marathon in four hours 41 minutes and going on to complete over 156 ultras and marathons.

pending_qa.q: What are the key differences between Flancy Activewear and major competitors like Nike?
pending_qa.r: Flancy's primary differentiation is color and design diversity. While Nike primarily focuses on black and very plain colors, Flancy features an in-house designer creating bespoke, bright, colorful, and funky designs, with approximately 85 different designs in their current collection. Flancy won Women's Running magazine's Best Active Wear of the Year award, with Nike listed as runners-up.

pending_qa.q: What was the unexpected market demand that proved initial skepticism about skorts wrong?
pending_qa.r: When Nicky proposed launching with skorts, a sportswear designer told her there was a good reason people did not wear them because people would not buy them. However, when Flancy launched at the National Running Show at the NEC in January 2019, skorts became their number-one seller from day one, with more than 50% of all sales being skorts, used for running, walking, canyoning, cross-country, dog dancing, and pickleball.

pending_qa.q: How did Nicky transition from a 25-year career in pharmaceutical sales to launching a retail activewear business?
pending_qa.r: While working as a pharmaceutical representative specializing in oncology, Nicky became increasingly stressed by high pressure, constant weekend and evening work, and frustration about the lack of colorful running apparel. Her husband suggested she start her own company and provided funding by cashing in a pension and selling a house in France. She lasted only three to four months trying to run both careers simultaneously before leaving pharmaceutical sales to focus entirely on Flancy.

pending_qa.q: What community-building strategy has contributed to customer loyalty and brand advocacy?
pending_qa.r: Nicky and her designer Jan launched the Flanders Active Community on Facebook approximately eight years ago at customer request. The community has proven remarkably positive, requiring moderation of only one member in eight years, primarily because the demographic is women aged 35-55 who prioritize women supporting women. The community organizes park run meetups across the country and child running weekends that sell out within 24 hours.

pending_qa.q: What challenges does a boutique activewear brand face when competing against established multinational sportswear companies?
pending_qa.r: Nicky was told to prepare to close the business within two to five years, as that was reportedly the average lifespan for boutique activewear brands. The business operates with minimal staff—only Nicky, her husband, one lady for pick-and-pack operations, a freelance designer (Jan), and outsourced newsletter and SEO work. The market is described as extremely tough, though Flancy has survived and grown beyond industry expectations.
